name: Maniq
confidence_why: Wnuk & Burenhult 2014 and Wnuk 2016 state from their own fieldwork that Maniq stress falls invariably on the final syllable, and every one of the 114 stress-marked Ten-edn forms in Peterson 2012 has final primary stress, the only divergence being a single secondary-stress mark on one trisyllabic loanword.

Corroboration also checked in PDF pp. 84-87 = printed 62-65): p.62 "the final syllable is the most stable par…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and fixed on the final syllable of the word (the stable 'major' syllable, as across Aslian); pre-final syllables are unstressed with reduced, variable vowels; Thai loanwords are likewise final-stressed; no tone or register.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly: 'no secondary stress has been found' (Wnuk & Burenhult 2014: 972).
new_statements.exceptions: None to the final-syllable rule. Proclitics are unstressed and do not affect stress assignment of the host (Wnuk 2016: 65); reduplicative/prefixal pre-final syllables are unstressed; function words unstressed in connected speech but stressed in isolation (2014: 964).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phonology article based on first-hand fieldwork (Wnuk) among Maniq of Satun/Trang/Phatthalung provinces, southern Thailand; phonetic transcriptions mark stress on the final syllable e.g. [pʌ̃ŋ-'pɛɡŋ] 'cheek'. No instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Maniq (autonym maniʔ; also known as Tonga, Mos, Ten'en/Ten-edn, 'Sakai' of Trang/Satun/Phatthalung, southern Thailand), ISO tnz = Glottolog tong1308; Wnuk's fieldwork is with the nomadic Maniq groups of the Banthad mountains (Satun/Trang/Phatthalung). Distinct from Kensiw (kens1248) of Yala, which Bishop 1996 confusingly also labelled 'Maniq'.

new_statements.quote: The examples given in these notes are written phonetically, using the IPA system. The phonetic inventory of sounds in Ten-edn are similar to those used in Kensiw5 as seen in Table 1 and 2. Primary stress and secondary stress have been marked, as in [biˈʔɛh] ‘money’ and [tə˞ˌmaˈgaʔ] ‘silver’. [fn. 5: Phonological information is taken from Bishop (1996).] [fn. 7, p. 23: The application of Ten-edn phonology varied among the different speakers, i.e. some closed the vowel at the end of a word with a consonant while others did not, e.g. sɯ ~ sɯh 'to buy'. Likewise, most Ten-edn speakers dropped tones from the Thai words.]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog rule (final stress) and with Wnuk & Burenhult 2014 p. 972 (stress invariably final, no secondary stress found). It adds, from transcriptions only, that (a) 114/114 stress-marked forms in a 1992-2003 ten-location survey of Ten-edn (plus some Kensiw forms) have final primary stress, (b) one trisyllabic loan is marked with initial secondary stress, which slightly diverges from Wnuk & Burenhult's 'no secondary stress has been found', and (c) Thai tones are mostly dropped in loans. Because the article never states a placement rule, it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog on its own authority; the phonological information it relies on (fn. 5) is Bishop 1996, a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article states no rule: it only says primary and secondary stress are marked in its IPA transcriptions and gives two examples, both with primary stress on the final syllable. Tallying every stress-marked token in the article (Ten-edn and Kensiw forms together): 114 tokens carry a primary-stress mark and all 114 have it on the final syllable (e.g. biˈʔɛh, baˈtuʔ, ʔuˈɟadn, kʌʎˈto̝gŋ, tɛnˈɛdn); none has it elsewhere. So the data imply fixed final primary stress, but this is a pattern read off transcriptions, not a statement by the author. The footnote that Ten-edn speakers mostly drop the tones of Thai loans confirms the language is not tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked in only one form, [tə˞ˌmaˈgaʔ] 'silver' (Malay tembaga), where secondary stress sits on the first syllable of a trisyllable; no rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Two-word phrases such as ˈpʰaː ˈhom carry a primary mark on each word. Thai loans appear with Thai tone marks in a few forms (sɯ́ː 'buy') but fn. 7 says most speakers drop the tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Peterson's 'Ten-edn (Tonga-Mos)' is the self-designation of the language of the Maniq of Trang, Satun and Phatthalung, i.e. the variety Wnuk & Burenhult 2014 call Maniq (tong1308); Peterson uses 'Maniq' for the people and 'Ten-edn' for the language. The article also contains Kensiw (Yala province; Glottolog kens1248) forms, kept in separate table rows, and its phonological inventory is explicitly taken from Bishop 1996, a Kensiw description. The stress tally above mixes Ten-edn and Kensiw tokens; both show only final primary stress.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Peterson 2012 marks secondary stress on one trisyllabic loan ([tə˞ˌmaˈgaʔ] 'silver'), whereas Wnuk & Burenhult 2014 (p. 972) say no secondary stress has been found in Maniq; that is a minor divergence in transcription practice on a single loanword, not a different placement of primary stress. Primary stress is final in every marked form in Peterson and 'invariably on the final syllable' per Wnuk & Burenhult 2014 and Wnuk 2016.
